etymology: Webster 1828 treats TOWARD / TOWARDS as preposition from Latin versus, verto: in the direction to; with direction to in a moral sense (with respect to / regarding); with ideal tendency to; and nearly. He illustrates from Numbers 24:1 (face toward the wilderness), Deuteronomy 28, and Acts 24 (conscience void of offense toward God and toward men). As adjective: ready to do or learn; not froward; apt, as a toward youth. As adverb: near; at hand; in a state of preparation. This page fills the KJV-gap preposition of direction and regard. Companion pages already treat east, lord, and christ.
biblical_def: Toward in Scripture is not a vibe and not a brand of openness. It names the face set, the eyes fixed, and the press of a man who has a mark. The psalmist will not let worship float: in thy fear will I worship toward thy holy temple (Psa 5:7). He will not let the glance wander: Mine eyes are ever toward the LORD (Psa 25:15). Mercy is not a mood: great is thy mercy toward me (Psa 86:13). The apostle will not baptize aimless motion: I press toward the mark for the prize of the high calling of God in Christ Jesus (Php 3:14). Love is not a circle of the already-liked: increase and abound in love one toward another, and toward all men (1Th 3:12). The dictionary therefore keeps toward from becoming either a compass without a Lord or a warmth without a temple. It is the Bible’s way of saying: this way — to Him.
webster_summary: Webster 1828 defines TOWARD / TOWARDS as preposition: in the direction to; with moral respect to; with tendency to; nearly. Adjective: ready to do or learn; apt. Adverb: near; at hand. He cites Numbers 24:1 and Acts 24.
webster_full: TO'WARDS, preposition [Latin versus, verto.]
1. In the direction to. He set his face toward the wilderness. Numbers 24:1.
2. With direction to, in a moral sense; with respect to; regarding. Herein do I exercise myself to have always a conscience void of offense toward God and toward men. Acts 24.
Hearing of thy love and faith which thou hast toward the Lord Jesus Christ, and toward all saints. Philemon 5.
3. With ideal tendency to.
4. Nearly.
TO'WARD / TO'WARDS, adverb Near; at hand; in a state of preparation.
TO'WARD, adjective Ready to do or learn; not froward; apt; as a toward youth.
scriptures: Psa 5:7
But as for me, I will come into thy house in the multitude of thy mercy: and in thy fear will I worship toward thy holy temple.
Mine eyes are ever toward the LORD; for he shall pluck my feet out of the net.
For great is thy mercy toward me: and thou hast delivered my soul from the lowest hell.
Php 3:14
I press toward the mark for the prize of the high calling of God in Christ Jesus.
And the Lord make you to increase and abound in love one toward another, and toward all men, even as we do toward you:
corruption_summary: Toward is corrupted when direction is emptied of the temple, when eyes-toward-the-LORD is recast as mindfulness, and when pressing toward the mark is sold as self-actualization.
corruption_paragraphs: The first corruption is direction without a holy place. Psalm 5:7 worships toward thy holy temple. The age keeps the preposition and drops the house. Openness is not worship. The recovery is fear in His courts.
The second corruption is Psalm 25:15 as a wellness glance. Mine eyes are ever toward the LORD is petition, not a breathing exercise. The net is real. The plucking is His.

The third corruption is Philippians 3:14 as a brand. I press toward the mark for the prize of the high calling of God in Christ Jesus is not a vision board. The mark is Christ’s calling, not a self-script. Love in 1 Thessalonians 3:12 runs toward all men because the Lord makes it increase — not because the circle voted.

usage: Worship is toward the holy temple in fear (Psa 5:7).
Eyes stay toward the LORD (Psa 25:15); mercy is toward the psalmist (Psa 86:13).
The apostle presses toward the mark in Christ (Php 3:14); love abounds one toward another (1Th 3:12).

etymology: Webster 1828 treats LEFT first as preterit and participle passive of leave, then as adjective from Latin lavus (Greek allied): the weak arm as opposed to the right, the strong or dextrous, whence the old note of sinister attached to that side. 1. Denoting the part opposed to the right of the body; as the left hand, arm, or side. 2. The left bank of a river is that on the left hand of a person facing the mouth. This page fills the KJV-gap adjective of the weak hand and the participle of what remains. Companion pages already treat right, hand, and man.
biblical_def: Left in Scripture is not a party and not a compliment. It names the weaker hand, the goats at the judgment, and what remains when a man has gone. Abram will not let the land become a quarrel: if thou wilt take the left hand, then I will go to the right (Gen 13:9). The King will not mix the flocks: he shall set the sheep on his right hand, but the goats on the left (Mat 25:33). Alms will not advertise: let not thy left hand know what thy right hand doeth (Mat 6:3). Peter will not leave the Holy One in the pit: his soul was not left in hell, neither his flesh did see corruption (Act 2:31). The first disciples will not keep the trade: they straightway left their nets, and followed him (Mat 4:20). The dictionary therefore keeps left from becoming either a mascot or a shrug. It is the Bible’s way of saying: the other hand — and what you must quit.
webster_summary: Webster 1828 defines LEFT as the preterit and participle of leave, and as adjective: the part opposed to the right of the body, the weaker arm; also the left bank of a river as seen facing the mouth.
webster_full: LEFT, preterit tense and participle passive of leave.

LEFT, adjective [Latin lavus; Gr. probably from the root of leave, Gr. and properly weak, deficient. Applied to the hand or arm, it denotes the weak arm, as opposed to the right, the strong or dextrous. Hence the ancient idea of sinister, unfortunate, attached to the left arm or side.]
1. Denoting the part opposed to the right of the body; as the left hand, arm or side. Hence, the noun being omitted, we say, on the left that is, on the left side or wing, as of an army.
2. The left bank of a river, is that which is on the left hand of a person whose face is towards the mouth of the river.
scriptures: Gen 13:9

Is not the whole land before thee? separate thyself, I pray thee, from me: if thou wilt take the left hand, then I will go to the right; or if thou depart to the right hand, then I will go to the left.
Mat 6:3
But when thou doest alms, let not thy left hand know what thy right hand doeth:
Mat 4:20
And they straightway left their nets, and followed him.
And he shall set the sheep on his right hand, but the goats on the left.
Act 2:31
He seeing this before spake of the resurrection of Christ, that his soul was not left in hell, neither his flesh did see corruption.
corruption_summary: Left is corrupted when the goats of Matthew 25 are recast as a political mascot, when the weak hand is baptized as identity, and when leaving the nets is sold as self-care rather than following.
corruption_paragraphs: The first corruption is Matthew 25 as a team jersey. The King sets sheep on the right and goats on the left. That is judgment, not a caucus. The dictionary will not let a modern wing steal the verse.

The second corruption is the weak arm as a self. Webster notes the left as the deficient arm. Scripture uses it without apology. Identity talk that baptizes the adjective as a people is not Genesis 13:9, where Abram yields a hand so the land will not become a fight.

The third corruption is leaving as therapy. Matthew 4:20 left their nets to follow Him. Acts 2:31 is Christ not left in hell. The participle is not a spa. One quits a trade; One does not see corruption.
roots_summary: Webster: preterit of leave; Latin lavus, the weak arm. Verse-cache Strong’s on the quotations below: Greek euonumos (G2176) at Matthew 25:33 on the left; Greek kataleipo (G2641) at Acts 2:31 on left. Genesis 13:9, Matthew 6:3, and Matthew 4:20 carry no Strong’s tag on left in this cache; this page does not mint one.
roots_lines: Greek euonumos (G2176) — of good name used as a euphemism for the left side (Mat 25:33, goats on the left).
Greek kataleipo (G2641) — to leave behind (Act 2:31, not left in hell).
Genesis 13:9, Matthew 6:3, and Matthew 4:20 are KJV-verified; the cache does not tag English left with a number on those verse lines. No lemma is invented here.
usage: Abram yields the left hand rather than quarrel (Gen 13:9).
Alms hide the left hand (Mat 6:3); disciples left their nets (Mat 4:20).
Goats stand on the left at the throne (Mat 25:33); Christ was not left in hell (Act 2:31).

etymology: Webster 1828 treats CUT as verb transitive (preterit and participle cut), from a root allied to Latin thrust / drive / strike: to separate parts by an edged instrument; to hew; to carve; to divide; to penetrate; to intersect. Phrasal: cut asunder (Psa 129:4), cut down groves (Exo 34:13), cut off as destroy / extirpate (1Ki 18:4; Psa 37). Noun: stroke, gash, channel, near passage, fashion of a garment. This page fills the KJV-gap verb of severance. Companion pages already treat wicked, hand, and earth.
biblical_def: Cut in Scripture is not a style and not a joke. It names the LORD’s severance of evildoers, the hand that must go rather than the whole body, and the cords of the wicked snapped. The psalmist will not let the wicked keep the land: evildoers shall be cut off: but those that wait upon the LORD, they shall inherit the earth (Psa 37:9). He will not let iniquity linger: the LORD our God shall cut them off (Psa 94:23). The Lord will not let a member veto the man: if thy right hand offend thee, cut it off (Mat 5:30). Paul will not let grafted pride forget the axe: otherwise thou also shalt be cut off (Rom 11:22). The righteous LORD hath cut asunder the cords of the wicked (Psa 129:4). The dictionary therefore keeps cut from becoming either a fashion or a cruelty-charge against God. It is the Bible’s way of saying: this far — and no farther.
webster_summary: Webster 1828 defines CUT as to separate by an edged instrument; to hew; to divide; to pierce. To cut off is to destroy or extirpate (Psa 37). To cut asunder is to sever (Psa 129:4). Noun: stroke, gash, channel, fashion.
webster_full: CUT, verb transitive preterit tense and preposition cut [Latin, to thrust, to drive, to strike.]

1. To separate the parts of any body by an edged instrument, either by striking, as with an ax, or by sawing or rubbing; to make a gash, incision or notch. Ye shall not cut yourselves. Deuteronomy 14:1.
2. To hew. Thy servants can skill to cut timber. 2 Chronicles 2:8.
To cut asunder, to cut into pieces; to divide; to sever. He hath cut asunder the cords of the wicked. Psalms 129:4.
To cut off, to separate one part from another; to destroy; to extirpate; to put to death untimely. Jezebel cut off the prophets of the Lord. 1 Kings 18:4. Evil doers shall be cut off. Psalms 37.
CUT, noun The action of an edged instrument; a cleft; a gash; a channel; a near passage; manner in which a thing is cut; form; shape; fashion.
scriptures: Psa 37:9
For evildoers shall be cut off: but those that wait upon the LORD, they shall inherit the earth.
And he shall bring upon them their own iniquity, and shall cut them off in their own wickedness; yea, the LORD our God shall cut them off.
The LORD is righteous: he hath cut asunder the cords of the wicked.
Mat 5:30
And if thy right hand offend thee, cut it off, and cast it from thee: for it is profitable for thee that one of thy members should perish, and not that thy whole body should be cast into hell.
Behold therefore the goodness and severity of God: on them which fell, severity; but toward thee, goodness, if thou continue in his goodness: otherwise thou also shalt be cut off.
corruption_summary: Cut is corrupted when the LORD’s cutting-off is called cruelty, when Matthew 5 is turned into self-harm counsel, and when being cut off from the tree is treated as a branding problem rather than severity.
corruption_paragraphs: The first corruption is Psalm 37 as embarrassment. Evildoers shall be cut off is promise to those who wait. Sentiment wants the earth without the axe. The recovery is that the LORD inherits the meek and severs the wicked.

The second corruption is Matthew 5:30 as a crisis-hotline verse. Cut it off is hyperbolic holiness against a member that offends — not a command to wound the body. The aim is not hell. The dictionary will not let the age steal the line either as gore or as joke.

The third corruption is Romans 11:22 without severity. Goodness toward the graft holds if thou continue; otherwise thou also shalt be cut off. Pride in the tree is the thing the axe is for. Psalm 129:4 is the LORD cutting cords, not a self-help unfollowing.

usage: The LORD cuts off in wickedness (Psa 94:23) and cuts asunder cords (Psa 129:4).
A hand that offends is cut off (Mat 5:30); the proud graft is cut off (Rom 11:22).

etymology: Webster 1828 treats ROUND as adjective: cylindrical, circular, spherical; full; smooth-flowing; plain / candid; brisk; plump. As noun: a circle; action in a circle; rotation in office; the step of a ladder; a watch performed about a garrison; a discharge of fire-arms. As adverb / preposition: on all sides; about (Luke 19:43, compass thee round). As verb: to make circular; to surround. This page fills the KJV-gap of what encircles. Companion pages already treat mountain, angel, and jerusalem.
biblical_def: Round in Scripture is not a meeting and not a brand of completeness. It names what encircles a people, for shelter or for siege. The wilderness will not let bread be a theory: there lay a small round thing, as small as the hoar frost on the ground (Exo 16:14). The psalmist will not let fear stand unguarded: The angel of the LORD encampeth round about them that fear him, and delivereth them (Psa 34:7). Geography preaches: As the mountains are round about Jerusalem, so the LORD is round about his people (Psa 125:2). Zechariah will not let the unwalled city panic: I, saith the LORD, will be unto her a wall of fire round about (Zec 2:5). Luke will not let the same word stay only comfort: enemies compass thee round (Luk 19:43). The dictionary therefore keeps round from becoming either a committee or a charm. It is the Bible’s way of saying: around you — either the LORD, or the trench.
webster_summary: Webster 1828 defines ROUND as circular or spherical; full; candid. Noun: a circle; a course returning to its start; a watch about a garrison. Adverb/preposition: on all sides; about (Luke 19:43). Verb: to make circular; to surround.
webster_full: ROUND, adjective 1. Cylindrical; circular; spherical or globular.
2. Full; large; as a round sum or price.
4. Plain; open; candid; fair. ROUND dealing is the honor of man's nature.
ROUND, noun A circle; a circular thing; action or performance in a circle; rotation in office; a rundle; the step of a ladder; a walk performed by a guard round a garrison.
ROUND, adverb 1. On all sides. Thine enemies shall cast a trench about thee, and compass thee round. Luke 19:43.
ROUND, preposition On every side of; as, the people stood round him.
ROUND, verb transitive To make circular, spherical or cylindrical; to surround; to encircle; to encompass.
scriptures: And when the dew that lay was gone up, behold, upon the face of the wilderness there lay a small round thing, as small as the hoar frost on the ground.
Psa 34:7
The angel of the LORD encampeth round about them that fear him, and delivereth them.
As the mountains are round about Jerusalem, so the LORD is round about his people from henceforth even for ever.
Zec 2:5
For I, saith the LORD, will be unto her a wall of fire round about, and will be the glory in the midst of her.
For the days shall come upon thee, that thine enemies shall cast a trench about thee, and compass thee round, and keep thee in on every side,
corruption_summary: Round is corrupted when the LORD-round-about is recast as a support circle, when manna’s small round thing is treated as a lifestyle snack, and when Luke 19’s compass-round is ignored so that encircling always means safety.
corruption_paragraphs: The first corruption is Psalm 34 as a group. The angel of the LORD encamps round about them that fear him. Fear of the LORD, not a facilitated circle, is the condition. The recovery is a holy encampment, not a roundtable.

The second corruption is Exodus 16 as branding. The small round thing is manna, bread from heaven, measured and for the day. It is not artisan completeness. Hunger is answered by the LORD, not by shape.

The third corruption is one-sided encircling. Psalm 125 and Zechariah 2 are the LORD round about as mountains and fire. Luke 19:43 is enemies who compass thee round. The same geometry can be siege. Comfort without that verse is a lie.

The angel encamps round about them that fear (Psa 34:7); mountains and the LORD are round about His people (Psa 125:2).
The LORD is a wall of fire round about (Zec 2:5); enemies also compass round (Luk 19:43).

etymology: Webster 1828 treats YOUNG (Yung) as adjective: not having been long born; being in the first part of life; not old; used of animals; being in the first part of growth, as a young plant; ignorant / weak, or rather having little experience. As noun: the offspring of animals, a single animal or offspring collectively. This page fills the KJV-gap adjective of the first part of life. Companion pages already treat old, child, and youth.
biblical_def: Young in Scripture is not a market and not an excuse. It names the first years under God, the man who must cleanse his way, and the strength that is still glory only if it is His. The psalmist will not let gray hair write a different providence: I have been young, and now am old; yet have I not seen the righteous forsaken (Psa 37:25). The BETH of Psalm 119 will not let the lad invent a path: Wherewithal shall a young man cleanse his way? by taking heed thereto according to thy word (Psa 119:9). Paul will not let the young men stay silly: Young men likewise exhort to be sober minded (Tit 2:6). John will not flatten the church into one age: I write unto you, young men, because ye have overcome the wicked one (1Jn 2:13). The proverb will not steal their strength for vanity: The glory of young men is their strength: and the beauty of old men is the gray head (Pro 20:29). The dictionary therefore keeps young from becoming either a cult or a slight. It is the Bible’s way of saying: early years — under the Word.
webster_summary: Webster 1828 defines YOUNG as not long born; in the first part of life or growth; of little experience. Noun: the offspring of animals, singly or together.
webster_full: YOUNG, adjective Yung. [G., Latin]
1. Not having been long born; being in the first part of life; not old; used of animals; as a young child; a young man; a young fawn.
2. Being in the first part of growth; as a young plant; a young tree.
3. Ignorant; weak; or rather, having little experience.
YOUNG, noun The offspring of animals, either a single animal, or offspring collectively. The cow will take care of her young as will the hen. Animals make provision for their young.
scriptures: I have been young, and now am old; yet have I not seen the righteous forsaken, nor his seed begging bread.
Wherewithal shall a young man cleanse his way? by taking heed thereto according to thy word.
Tit 2:6
Young men likewise exhort to be sober minded.

I write unto you, fathers, because ye have known him that is from the beginning. I write unto you, young men, because ye have overcome the wicked one. I write unto you, little children, because ye have known the Father.
The glory of young men is their strength: and the beauty of old men is the gray head.
corruption_summary: Young is corrupted when youth is treated as a separate gospel, when Psalm 119’s cleansing-by-the-Word is replaced with self-expression, and when strength is baptized as a right to delay repentance.
corruption_paragraphs: The first corruption is a youth church. Psalm 37:25 is one providence from young to old. The righteous are not forsaken at either end. Segmented religion that gives the young a different Christ is not this verse.
The second corruption is Psalm 119:9 without the Word. A young man cleanses his way by taking heed to the Word, not by finding his voice. Expression is not holiness.

The third corruption is strength as delay. Proverbs 20:29 names the glory of young men as strength; Titus 2:6 tells them to be sober minded; 1 John 2:13 says they have overcome the wicked one. Strength is for war under the Word, not for a longer childhood.

A young man cleanses his way by the Word (Psa 119:9); young men are to be sober (Tit 2:6).
Young men overcome the wicked one (1Jn 2:13); their glory is strength (Pro 20:29).
